claim: RNA polymerases (RNAPs) contain a conserved 'secondary channel' which binds regulatory factors that modulate transcription initiation.
source: RNA polymerases (RNAPs) contain a conserved 'secondary channel' which binds regulatory factors that modulate transcription initiation.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about RNAP structure and function.

claim: GreB arrived and departed from promoters only in complex with RNAP.
source: GreB arrived and departed from promoters only in complex with RNAP.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the single-molecule observations described in the manuscript.

claim: GreB did not alter initial RNAP-promoter binding but instead blocked a step after conformational rearrangement of the initial RNAP-promoter complex.
source: GreB did not alter initial RNAP-promoter binding but instead blocked a step after conformational rearrangement of the initial RNAP-promoter complex.
evidence: This conclusion is based on experimental data showing no change in binding rates but inhibition of initiation.

claim: GreB-RNAP complexes never initiated at an rRNA promoter; only RNAP molecules arriving at the promoter without bound GreB produced transcript.
source: Strikingly, GreB-RNAP complexes never initiated at an rRNA promoter; only RNAP molecules arriving at the promoter without bound GreB produced transcript.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the single-molecule experiments.

claim: rRNA promoters are inhibited by GreB/DksA because their short-lived RNAP complexes do not allow sufficient time for SCFs to dissociate.
source: The data reveal that a model SCF functions by a 'delayed inhibition' mechanism and suggest that rRNA promoters are inhibited by GreB/DksA because their short-lived RNAP complexes do not allow sufficient time for SCFs to dissociate.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the experimental observations.

claim: Multi-subunit RNA polymerases (RNAPs) contain catalytic subunits that are conserved across all domains of life.
source: Multi-subunit RNA polymerases (RNAPs), the molecular machines responsible for the synthesis of cellular mRNAs, contain catalytic subunits that are conserved across all domains of life (Cramer, 2002; Werner and Grohmann, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The secondary channel is a pore that provides access to the deeply-buried active site of the enzyme.
source: An important such regulatory hot spot is the secondary channel, a pore that provides access to the deeply-buried active site of the enzyme (Nickels and Hochschild, 2004).
evidence: This is a structural description supported by a citation.

claim: Two evolutionarily distinct SCF families have evolved in bacteria and eukaryotes, distinguished by insertion into the channel of either antiparallel α-helices (bacteria; GreA-like proteins) or of a β hairpin (eukaryotes, TFIIS-like proteins).
source: Two evolutionarily distinct SCF families have evolved in bacteria and eukaryotes, distinguished by insertion into the channel of either antiparallel α-helices (bacteria; GreA-like proteins) or of a β hairpin (eukaryotes, TFIIS-like proteins).
evidence: This is a statement of established structural knowledge about SCF families.

claim: Escherichia coli uses at least five distinct GreA-like SCFs.
source: Escherichia coli uses at least five distinct GreA-like SCFs (Zenkin and Yuzenkova, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: GreB stimulates endonucleolytic cleavage of the nascent transcript in transcription elongation complexes (ECs).
source: GreB, for example, was first identified as an SCF that stimulates endonucleolytic cleavage of the nascent transcript in transcription elongation complexes (ECs).
evidence: This is a well-established function of GreB supported by citations.

claim: GreB stimulates cleavage of RNA that has reverse threaded through the active site (backtracked) by multiple nucleotides.
source: GreB stimulates cleavage of RNA that has reverse threaded through the active site (backtracked) by multiple nucleotides, for instance after nucleotide misincorporation at the RNA 3′ end (Borukhov et al., 2001; Borukhov et al., 1993; Laptenko et al., 2003).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: GreB and GreA can stimulate transcription by aiding promoter escape.
source: By causing removal of the backtracked segment of the nascent transcript both GreB and its paralog, GreA, can stimulate transcription by aiding promoter escape (Duchi et al., 2016; Feng et al., 1994; Hsu et al., 1995; Lerner et al., 2016; Shimamoto et al., 1986; Susa et al., 2002)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: GreB and GreA can stimulate transcription by allowing escape from promoter-proximal σ70-paused ECs.
source: By causing removal of the backtracked segment of the nascent transcript both GreB and its paralog, GreA, can stimulate transcription by aiding promoter escape (Duchi et al., 2016; Feng et al., 1994; Hsu et al., 1995; Lerner et al., 2016; Shimamoto et al., 1986; Susa et al., 2002) and by allowing escape from promoter-proximal σ70-paused ECs (Deighan et al., 2011; Marr and Roberts, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: GreB (but not GreA) can inhibit initiation by RNAP prior to phosphodiester bond formation at certain promoters with short-lived RNAP-promoter complexes such as the ribosomal RNA (rRNA) rrnB P1 promoter.
source: In contrast, GreB (but not GreA) also can inhibit initiation by RNAP prior to phosphodiester bond formation at certain promoters with short-lived RNAP-promoter complexes such as the ribosomal RNA (rRNA) rrnB P1 promoter (Rutherford et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: DksA has a divergent domain that binds outside the secondary channel.
source: This GreB activity is similar to one of the activities of a different E. coli SCF, DksA, which has a divergent domain that binds outside the secondary channel.
evidence: This is a structural description of DksA.

claim: DksA does not promote transcript cleavage.
source: DksA does not promote transcript cleavage and has other effects on transcript elongation (Zenkin and Yuzenkova, 2015; Zhang et al., 2014)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: DksA can strongly affect initiation either negatively at 'stringent' promoters (e.g., rrnB P1) or positively at other promoters (e.g., the histidine biosynthetic operon promoter PhisG).
source: DksA does not promote transcript cleavage and has other effects on transcript elongation (Zenkin and Yuzenkova, 2015; Zhang et al., 2014), but it can strongly affect initiation either negatively at 'stringent' promoters (e.g., rrnB P1) or positively at other promoters (e.g., the histidine biosynthetic operon promoter PhisG) (Gourse et al., 2018; Paul et al., 2005; Paul et al., 2004; Potrykus et al., 2006; Rutherford et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Production of rRNA is suppressed during the stringent response, a global reprogramming of gene expression in response to amino acid starvation.
source: Production of rRNA is suppressed during the stringent response, a global reprogramming of gene expression in response to amino acid starvation (Browning and Busby, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: DksA binds in the SC and reduces initiation from rrnB P1 during the stringent response.
source: DksA binds in the SC and reduces initiation from rrnB P1 during the stringent response (Paul et al., 2004; Ross et al., 2016; Rutherford et al., 2009; Rutherford et al., 2007)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The effect of DksA on rrnB P1 initiation is potentiated by binding of guanosine tetraphosphate (ppGpp), which is accumulated at concentrations up to ~1 mM to signal amino acid starvation.
source: DksA binds in the SC and reduces initiation from rrnB P1 during the stringent response (Paul et al., 2004; Ross et al., 2016; Rutherford et al., 2009; Rutherford et al., 2007); this effect is potentiated by binding of guanosine tetraphosphate (ppGpp), which is accumulated at concentrations up to ~1 mM to signal amino acid starvation.
evidence: This statement describes the role of ppGpp in the stringent response.

claim: ppGpp binds two sites on RNAP to modulate transcription: one at the interface of the omega and β′ subunits and a second created by DksA upon binding in the SC.
source: ppGpp binds two sites on RNAP to modulate transcription: one at the interface of the omega and β′ subunits and a second created by DksA upon binding in the SC (Molodtsov et al., 2018; Ross et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Cells must maintain appropriate levels of rRNA during rapid-growth (i.e., non-starvation) conditions, conditions in which rRNAs are the most abundant transcripts produced.
source: Although much study has focused on stringent regulation of rRNA production, cells must also maintain appropriate levels of rRNA during rapid-growth (i.e., non-starvation) conditions, conditions in which rRNAs are the most abundant transcripts produced.
evidence: This is a statement of biological knowledge about rRNA regulation.

claim: A growth rate-dependent control system maintains rRNA levels relative to total cellular protein by making rRNA synthesis proportional to the steady-state growth rate rather than to amino acid availability.
source: A growth rate-dependent control (Bartlett and Gourse, 1994) system maintains rRNA levels relative to total cellular protein by making rRNA synthesis proportional to the steady-state growth rate rather than to amino acid availability (Gourse et al., 1986; Josaitis et al., 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Growth rate-dependent regulation occurs at micromolar cellular concentrations of ppGpp rather than the millimolar concentrations that mediate stringent regulation.
source: This regulation occurs at micromolar cellular concentrations of ppGpp (Ross et al., 2016; Ryals et al., 1982) rather than the millimolar concentrations that mediate stringent regulation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: There is potential for involvement of both GreB and DksA in growth rate dependent control.
source: In contrast to stringent regulation of rRNA transcription (in which DksA is clearly implicated), there is potential for involvement of both GreB and DksA in growth rate dependent control (Mallik et al., 2006; Rutherford et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: The mechanism for growth rate-dependent control of rRNA synthesis by the two SCFs is unknown.
source: The mechanism for growth rate-dependent control of rRNA synthesis by the two SCFs is unknown, and the point in the transcription cycle at which the SCFs load onto RNAP has not been defined.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: The point in the transcription cycle at which the SCFs load onto RNAP has not been defined.
source: The mechanism for growth rate-dependent control of rRNA synthesis by the two SCFs is unknown, and the point in the transcription cycle at which the SCFs load onto RNAP has not been defined.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: GreB binds both core and σ70RNAP with KD = 10 ± 1 nM.
source: A hyperbolic fit to the fraction bound data at varying σ70RNAP concentrations revealed tight binding with KD = 10 ± 1 nM (Figure 1C). Similar experiments performed with core RNAP again yielded KD = 10 ± 1 nM (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from FCS experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: GreB binds both core and σ70RNAP an order of magnitude more tightly than was estimated in previous non-equilibrium measurements of binding.
source: These measurements demonstrate that GreB binds both core and σ70RNAP an order of magnitude more tightly than was estimated in previous non-equilibrium measurements of binding (Furman et al., 2013; Loizos and Darst, 1999; Rutherford et al., 2007)
evidence: This is a comparison of the current measurements to prior literature.

claim: GreB binds both core and σ70RNAP an order of magnitude more tightly than previously measured for GreB binding to ECs.
source: These measurements demonstrate that GreB binds both core and σ70RNAP an order of magnitude more tightly than was estimated in previous non-equilibrium measurements of binding (Furman et al., 2013; Loizos and Darst, 1999; Rutherford et al., 2007) and an order of magnitude more tightly than previously measured for GreB binding to ECs (Tetone et al., 2017; Table 1).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior measurements, with reference to Table 1.

claim: The dissociation constant for GreB interaction with RNAP is ~10 fold tighter than the values reported for DksA in the absence of ppGpp.
source: The dissociation constant for the interaction is also ~10 fold tighter than the values reported for DksA in the absence of ppGpp (KD = 101 ± 19 or 112 [no S.E. reported] nM for core, KD = 99 ± 15 or 52 [no S.E. reported] nM for σ70 holoenzyme) (Lennon et al., 2009; Molodtsov et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison to literature values for DksA binding.

claim: GreBCy3 binding to σ70RNAP was quantitatively indistinguishable from that of unlabeled GreB, indicating that the high binding affinity is not an artefact of dye labeling.
source: GreBCy3 binding to σ70RNAP was quantitatively indistinguishable from that of unlabeled GreB (see Materials and methods), indicating that the high binding affinity is not an artefact of dye labeling.
evidence: This is a control experiment demonstrating that labeling does not affect binding.

claim: Addition of 10 nM GreB reduced the rate of initiation approximately four-fold.
source: Addition to the experiment of 10 nM GreB reduced the rate of initiation approximately four-fold (Figure 2C, purple vs. green curves; Figure 2G, leftmost two bars).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the CoSMoS experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: The inhibitory effect of DksA is identical to that of GreB (within experimental uncertainty) when measured at the same fractional occupancy of σ70RNAP.
source: Significantly, the inhibitory effect of DksA is identical to that of GreB (within experimental uncertainty) when we performed the analogous experiment with DksA at its KD in place of GreB. (Figure 2D; Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental results shown in Figure 2.

claim: GreB and DksA have indistinguishable inhibitory effects in the presence of 100 μM ppGpp.
source: We found similarly indistinguishable inhibitory effects of GreB and DksA in the presence of 100 μM ppGpp (Figure 2E–G; Rutherford et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a direct observation from experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: GreB inhibits initiation ~10 fold more potently than DksA on a concentration basis, but the difference can be fully accounted for by the difference in the binding affinities of the two proteins.
source: Thus, GreB inhibits initiation ~10 fold more potently than DksA on a concentration basis, but the difference can be fully accounted for by the difference in the binding affinities of the two proteins, without reference to any functional differences between GreB- and DksA-bound RNAP.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data comparing GreB and DksA.

claim: Some σ70RNAP647 molecules arrived at DNA locations in complex with GreBCy3B molecules, whereas others arrived without detectable GreBCy3B fluorescence.
source: In these three-color CoSMoS experiments, we observed that some σ70RNAP647 molecules arrived at DNA locations in complex with GreBCy3B molecules (orange highlights in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2), whereas others arrived without detectable GreBCy3B fluorescence (purple highlights).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the CoSMoS experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: The fraction of σ70RNAP647 molecules observed to arrive simultaneously with GreBCy3B agrees with that expected, demonstrating that σ70RNAP•GreBCy3B and σ70RNAP have similar rate constants for binding to DNA.
source: The fraction of σ70RNAP647 molecules observed to arrive simultaneously with GreBCy3B agrees with that expected (Figure 3C), demonstrating that σ70RNAP•GreBCy3B and σ70RNAP have similar rate constants for binding to DNA.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of observed and predicted fractions in Figure 3C.

claim: At 10 nM GreBCy3B, only 3.5 ± 0.9% of σ70RNAP•DNA complexes bind GreB.
source: In particular, at 10 nM GreBCy3B we saw only 3.5 ± 0.9% of σ70RNAP•DNA complexes bind GreB (47 instances of binding to 1,355 complexes over a summed duration of 1,121 s, corresponding to kon = (0.42 ± 0.06)×107 M−1 s−1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the CoSMoS experiments.

claim: GreB suppression of rrnB P1 initiation is essentially completely controlled by GreB binding to σ70RNAP off DNA rather than GreB binding to initiation complexes.
source: Thus these data suggest that GreB suppression of rrnB P1 initiation is essentially completely controlled by GreB binding to σ70RNAP off DNA rather than GreB binding to initiation complexes, and that this conclusion holds in both high (>>KD) and low (<<KD) GreB concentration regimes.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion based on the experimental observations.

claim: More than 90% of recorded σ70RNAP•GreB•DNA complexes ended with simultaneous departure of GreBCy3B and σ70RNAP647.
source: More than 90% of recorded σ70RNAP•GreB•DNA complexes ended with simultaneous departure of GreBCy3B and σ70RNAP647 (Figure 3D, orange highlight).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the CoSMoS experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There is no evidence for GreB dissociation that leaves behind polymerase bound to the promoter.
source: Thus, we see no evidence for GreB dissociation that leaves behind polymerase bound to the promoter.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the simultaneous departure observations.

claim: The extent of GreB inhibition of rrnB P1 initiation is quantitatively set by the amount of GreB holoenzyme occupancy.
source: The observations that GreB nearly always arrives at the promoter together with RNAP and only dissociates with RNAP suggest that the extent of GreB inhibition of rrnB P1 initiation is quantitatively set by the amount of GreB holoenzyme occupancy.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the experimental observations.

claim: Neither GreB nor DksA significantly altered ka, the second-order rate constant for initial binding of σ70RNAP647 to rrnB P1 DNA.
source: Even at concentrations at which half of the holoenzyme molecules are occupied, the CoSMoS data show that neither SCF significantly altered ka, the second-order rate constant for initial binding of σ70RNAP647 to rrnB P1 DNA (Figure 3E; Table 3).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the CoSMoS experiments shown in Figure 3E and Table 3.

claim: There was no substantial alteration of σ70RNAP647 dwell times on rrnB P1 when GreB or DksA was present.
source: However, we also saw no substantial alteration of σ70RNAP647 dwell times on rrnB P1 when GreB or DksA was present (Figure 3F; Table 3).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the CoSMoS experiments shown in Figure 3F and Table 3.

claim: The SCFs act at a step in initiation after formation of initial closed complexes, such as isomerization to open complex or subsequent nucleotide addition reactions.
source: Therefore, kinetic destabilization of the two resolvable closed complexes also cannot account for the observed inhibition of initiation from rrnB P1. Taken together, these data imply that the SCFs act at a step in initiation after formation of these initial closed complexes, such as isomerization to open complex or subsequent nucleotide addition reactions.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion based on the experimental observations.

claim: In none (zero of 39) of the productive binding events did RNAP arrive accompanied by GreB.
source: Strikingly, in none (zero of 39) of these productive binding events did RNAP arrive accompanied by GreB.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the four-color CoSMoS experiments.

claim: RNAP arrived together with GreB in hundreds (~50% of 1,755 total RNAP binding events) of non-productive RNAP binding events.
source: In contrast, RNAP arrived together with GreB in hundreds (~50% of 1,755 total RNAP binding events) of non-productive RNAP binding events.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the four-color CoSMoS experiments.

claim: σ70RNAP molecules that are complexed with GreB cannot initiate transcription on rrnB P1.
source: Taken together, these observations strongly suggest that σ70RNAP molecules that are complexed with GreB cannot initiate transcription on rrnB P1, and again show that GreB blockage of the rrnB initiation pathway occurs at a step after formation of the initial closed complex intermediates.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that no GreB-bound RNAP initiated transcription.

claim: GreB repression of initiation at a rRNA promoter does not affect the initial binding of RNAP to the promoter but modulates later step(s).
source: Proteins that regulate transcription initiation can do so by affecting the initial binding of RNAP to the promoter or by modulating later step(s) such as promoter complex isomerization, initial RNA synthesis, or promoter escape (Browning and Busby, 2016). In this study, we show that GreB repression of initiation at a rRNA promoter falls into the latter category.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: GreB presence on RNAP does not affect the formation of initial closed complexes, their stabilities, or their rates of dissociation.
source: We show by direct observation that GreB binds to free σ70RNAP in solution and its presence on RNAP does not affect the formation of initial closed complexes, their stabilities, or their rates of dissociation (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: Closed complexes with GreB bound were never observed to progress to ECs, indicating that the secondary channel factor presence introduces a barrier to initiation.
source: Instead, GreB acts at a later stage: closed complexes with GreB bound were never observed to progress to ECs, indicating that the secondary channel factor presence introduces a barrier to initiation at, for example, the closed-to-open complex isomerization stage or a subsequent step
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that GreB-bound RNAP never initiated.

claim: The barrier to initiation introduced by GreB is effectively insurmountable because it cannot be overcome on the time scale of rrnB P1 promoter complex lifetimes.
source: closed complexes with GreB bound were never observed to progress to ECs, indicating that the secondary channel factor presence introduces a barrier to initiation at, for example, the closed-to-open complex isomerization stage or a subsequent step; this barrier is effectively insurmountable because it cannot be overcome on the time scale of rrnB P1 promoter complex lifetimes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observations.

claim: GreB and DksA inhibit rrnB by similar mechanisms.
source: Our data suggest that GreB and DksA inhibit rrnB by similar mechanisms
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the similar inhibitory effects observed for both factors.

claim: The results are compatible with proposals that DksA inhibits rRNA synthesis at least in part by affecting isomerization or open complex decay.
source: Our data suggest that GreB and DksA inhibit rrnB by similar mechanisms, and the results are therefore compatible with proposals that DksA inhibits rRNA synthesis at least in part by affecting isomerization or open complex decay (Paul et al., 2005; Rutherford et al., 2009; Rutherford et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings to prior proposals in the literature.

claim: The data are consistent with a mechanism in which the two SCFs may additionally inhibit initiation by obstructing catalytic function of the open complex active site.
source: The data are also consistent with a mechanism inspired by structural data (e.g., Molodtsov et al., 2018) in which the two SCFs may additionally inhibit initiation by obstructing catalytic function of the open complex active site.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation consistent with structural data.

claim: GreB was almost never observed to bind to or depart from σ70RNAP-promoter complexes.
source: Perhaps unexpectedly for a factor affecting only later stage(s) of initiation, we find that GreB does not function by binding to rrnB promoter complexes during those stages. In our experiments, GreB was almost never observed to bind to or depart from σ70RNAP-promoter complexes.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the single-molecule experiments.

claim: GreB arrived only at promoters that were not already bound by σ70RNAP and arrived only in complex with σ70RNAP.
source: Instead, GreB arrived only at promoters that were not already bound by σ70RNAP and arrived only in complex with σ70RNAP.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the single-molecule experiments.

claim: GreB left the promoter only as a σ70RNAP•GreB complex.
source: Similarly, it left the promoter only as a σ70RNAP•GreB complex.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the single-molecule experiments.

claim: rRNA promoter complexes are atypically short lived.
source: However, rRNA promoter complexes are atypically short lived (Ruff et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: On more typical promoters, promoter complexes may be sufficiently long-lived to allow association of and dissociation of GreB.
source: On more typical promoters, promoter complexes may be sufficiently long-lived to allow association of and dissociation of GreB.
evidence: This is a speculation about behavior on other promoters based on the rrnB P1 findings.

claim: Dissociation of GreB during a long-lived promoter complex would prevent the suppression of initiation by the mechanism observed with rrnB P1, providing a straightforward explanation for why GreB (and DksA) selectively inhibits initiation at promoters that have short-lived promoter complexes.
source: Dissociation of GreB during a long-lived promoter complex would prevent the suppression of initiation by the mechanism we observe with rrnB P1, providing a straightforward explanation for why GreB (and DksA) selectively inhibits initiation at promoters that have short-lived promoter complexes (Paul et al., 2005; Rutherford et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on the experimental findings.

claim: On promoters with long-lived RNAP complexes, inhibition by this mechanism would be abolished or weakened, and stimulatory effects of Gre factors could act to accelerate initiation.
source: On promoters with long-lived RNAP complexes, inhibition by this mechanism would be abolished or weakened, and stimulatory effects of Gre factors (e.g., preventing abortive initiation [Chander et al., 2015; Duchi et al., 2016; Feng et al., 1994; Hsu et al., 1995; Lerner et al., 2016] or suppressing promoter-proximal pausing [Deighan et al., 2011; Marr and Roberts, 2000]) observed at some promoters could act to accelerate initiation.
evidence: This is a speculation about behavior on other promoters, supported by citations.

claim: Competition between SCFs for binding to σ70RNAP in solution (i.e., before it binds to promoter) may determine which SCFs are most important for rRNA transcription regulation under various growth conditions.
source: The demonstration that GreB occupancy of holoenzyme is what dictates GreB inhibition of rrnB suggests that competition between SCFs for binding to σ70RNAP in solution (i.e., before it binds to promoter) may determine which SCFs are most important for rRNA transcription regulation under various growth conditions.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: All three approaches (FCS, single-molecule kinetics, and fraction arriving/departing with DNA) showed that GreB binds σ70RNAP with a KD more than 10-fold tighter than its binding to ECs.
source: All three approaches showed that that GreB binds σ70RNAP with a KD more than 10-fold tighter than its binding to ECs (Table 1)
evidence: This is a summary of measurements from multiple experimental approaches.

claim: GreB binds σ70RNAP much tighter than prior estimates based on non-equilibrium studies of its affinity for core RNAP or initial transcription complexes.
source: All three approaches showed that that GreB binds σ70RNAP with a KD more than 10-fold tighter than its binding to ECs (Table 1) and much tighter than prior estimates based on non-equilibrium studies of its affinity for core RNAP or initial transcription complexes (Furman et al., 2013; Lennon et al., 2012; Lennon et al., 2009; Loizos and Darst, 1999; Rutherford et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior literature values.

claim: The tight binding affinity of GreB for holoenzyme is consistent with the observed potent inhibition of rrnB P1 initiation kinetics by low concentrations (10 nM) of GreB.
source: The tight binding affinity of GreB for holoenzyme is also consistent with the observed potent inhibition of rrnB P1 initiation kinetics by low concentrations (10 nM) of GreB.
evidence: This is a consistency check between binding affinity and functional effects.

claim: Since the binding of GreB to holoenzyme is much tighter than to ECs, holoenzyme molecules are likely able to at least partially compete with ECs for association with unbound GreB, even if the latter are present in significant excess.
source: Since the binding of GreB to holoenzyme is much tighter than to ECs, holoenzyme molecules are likely able to at least partially compete with ECs for association with unbound GreB, even if the latter are present in significant excess.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relative binding affinities.

claim: The relative importance of GreB and DksA in regulation of initiation at rrnB P1 is simply determined by which one dominates occupation of the secondary channel in the cellular pool of σ70RNAP.
source: Our observation that GreB binds to and releases from holoenzyme, not rRNA promoter complexes, provides strong support for the proposal (Rutherford et al., 2007) that the relative importance of GreB and DksA in regulation of initiation at rrnB P1 is simply determined by which one dominates occupation of the secondary channel in the cellular pool of σ70RNAP.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion supported by the experimental observations and a citation.

claim: Equilibrium occupancy is determined by both the binding affinities and the ratios of unbound (not total) SCF concentrations, which are not known.
source: Equilibrium occupancy is determined by both the binding affinities (measured here for GreB) and the ratios of unbound (not total) SCF concentrations, which are not known.
evidence: This is a statement about what determines equilibrium occupancy and identifies a knowledge gap.

claim: The two proteins (GreB and DksA) may have redundant functions in growth-rate dependent rRNA regulation.
source: The two proteins may have redundant functions in growth-rate dependent rRNA regulation, but the phenotypes of genetic deletion strains (Rutherford et al., 2007) are difficult to interpret unambiguously because of the other, non-overlapping functions of the two proteins in transcription elongation and other cellular processes (Furman et al., 2013; Furman et al., 2012; Tehranchi et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculation about functional redundancy, with citations to relevant literature.

claim: The millimolar levels of ppGpp present during the stringent response may selectively promote DksA binding over that of GreB.
source: In contrast, the millimolar levels of ppGpp present during the stringent response may selectively promote DksA binding over that of GreB (Molodtsov et al., 2018; Ross et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculation based on citations to prior work.

claim: DksA may become the dominant regulator of the two during amino acid starvation.
source: Thus, DksA may become the dominant regulator of the two during amino acid starvation.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the differential effects of ppGpp.

claim: Single-molecule kinetic measurements show a biexponential dwell time distribution of GreB on surface-tethered core and σ70RNAP, indicating distinct short- and long-lived classes of binding events.
source: Single-molecule kinetic measurements show a biexponential dwell time distribution of GreB on surface-tethered core and σ70RNAP (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D,F), indicating distinct short- and long-lived classes of binding events.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the single-molecule kinetic measurements.

claim: Only a very small fraction of GreB interactions with holoenzyme (11%) achieve the long-lived state.
source: Only a very small fraction of GreB interactions with holoenzyme (11%; calculated as (1 – a) from the value of a in Table 1) achieve the long-lived state, and what causes the different behaviors of the two classes is obscure.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the fit parameters in Table 1.

claim: Using GreB as a model SCF, transcription factor binding to free σ70RNAP, rather than to initiation complexes, is the critical factor that determines the relative importance of each SCF in inhibiting initiation from rRNA promoters.
source: Using GreB as a model SCF, we propose based on our data that transcription factor binding to free σ70RNAP, rather than to initiation complexes, is the critical factor that determines the relative importance of each SCF in inhibiting initiation from rRNA promoters.
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal based on the experimental findings.

claim: GreB functions by a 'delayed inhibition' mechanism.
source: The data reveal that GreB functions by a 'delayed inhibition' mechanism
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion based on the experimental observations.

claim: DksA functions by the same 'delayed inhibition' mechanism as GreB.
source: The data reveal that GreB functions by a 'delayed inhibition' mechanism, and imply that DksA functions by the same mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similar effects of GreB and DksA.

claim: The diffusion constant of GreBCy3 is 60 ± 10 μm2 s−1.
source: The autocorrelation curves for free GreBCy3 were fit to obtain a diffusion constant of 60 ± 10 μm2 s−1 (all uncertainties are SE unless otherwise indicated).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from FCS experiments.
